item.title: Intel shares are soaring by 10% in trading today.
item.description:
Intel shares are surging 10% today, helped by a combination of improving analyst sentiment, potential pricing power and increased optimism surrounding the company’s foundry business.

Northland Securities upgraded Intel to Outperform from Market Perform and established a $120 price target. Analyst Gus Richard pointed to improving execution in Intel’s turnaround, tight supplies of server processors and the potential benefit from the company’s reported involvement with Tesla’s Terafab semiconductor project.

If that relationship develops, it could provide an important boost for Intel Foundry, the division responsible for manufacturing chips for outside customers.

Separately, DigiTimes reported that Intel may raise CPU prices by as much as 10%. If demand remains firm and processor supplies stay constrained, higher prices could help Intel improve margins and strengthen its financial and manufacturing position.

Those fundamental developments have given buyers a reason to push the stock higher. However, the technical picture is what tells traders where the bullish bias remains intact—and where it begins to weaken.

Buyers started taking control last week

Intel shares fell below the 100-day moving average on August 18 and remained below that longer-term technical barometer as the price declined to $85.14 on August 24.

The first signs of a potential turnaround appeared last week. The price moved above its 100-hour moving average—currently at $91.27—on Thursday before extending above its 200-hour moving average at $94.72 on Friday.

Moving above both hourly moving averages shifted the short-term technical bias back in favor of the buyers. Those breaks did not guarantee that the price would continue higher, but they gave buyers greater control and provided the technical foundation for today’s sharp move.

The gap higher strengthens the bullish bias

Intel gapped higher today, with the low during the first hour of trading reaching $100.35. Holding above the psychologically important $100 level was the first positive signal.

The price subsequently moved above a swing level near $102.40 and the rising 100-day moving average at $104.27. Intel has now remained above its 100-day moving average for the past five trading hours.

That is important. The 100-day moving average represents a key dividing line between buyers and sellers. As long as the price remains above that level, the buyers are in firm control.

What are the next upside targets?

The next target comes at the August 13 swing high of $107.57. A sustained move above that level would open the door toward the 50% retracement of the decline from Intel’s June all-time high. That midpoint comes in at $112.05.

The price has not traded above those levels since July 9, making the area an important upside objective—and a likely test of whether today’s momentum can develop into a more sustained bullish move.

What would weaken the bullish picture?

For buyers, the rising 100-day moving average at $104.27 is now the closest risk-defining level. Staying above it keeps the technical bias firmly pointed higher.

A move back below the 100-day moving average would be a warning that some of today’s enthusiasm is beginning to fade. The next important support would then come near the former swing resistance at $102.40.

The bottom line is that the buyers are making a play. Above $104.27, they remain in firm control, with $107.57 followed by $112.05 as the next upside targets. A move back below $104.27—and particularly below $102.40—would weaken the bullish technical picture.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.description:

Crude rose at the open and climbed as high as $94.37 per barrel today but has now largely retreated and is up 88-cents to $92.30.

Earlier this hour, brent prices even turned briefly negative.

The chart here is where it gets interesting as today's move could be a false breakout above the June high. Oil has been consolidating near that levels but it's been losing momentum after a bit runup from $80. Today was a 'good news' day for oil but it wasn't able to complete the break. That begs the question: if it can't rally on good news, when can it?

The US struck three Iranian tankers on the weekend and sunk one. That was after Iran fired on US ships and US bases in the region. The Yemeni Houthis also struck and shut down some Saudi oil infrastructure on the weekend.

Overall though, I'm still bullish on oil. It's tough to pin down how much oil the Hormuz conflict is removing from the global market but it's a material number. China has dramatically slowed its imports and the US is using the SPR but that isn't sustainable so the squeeze is coming and it's going to take awhile to get everything running properly once it's all over. For now, the pain is being felt in record diesel prices but it won't be long until that works its way into crude.

item.title: Flights reportedly suspended at Jeddah airport in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
There were reports that flights have been suspended at Jeddah Airport in Saudi Arabia . There is other reports of explosions in Jazan region of Saudi Arabia with explosions heard in Saudi Arabian oilfields.   Alerts have also been activated in Saudi Arabia is Jazan region but reports are that the danger has passed. 

Tensions rise between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis

Tensions surrounding Saudi Arabia increased sharply over the weekend as fighting intensified between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels and forces aligned with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Saudi-backed forces expanded ground operations against the Houthis on several fronts, including Hodeida, Taiz, Jawf, Marib and Bayda. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of supporting airstrikes inside Yemen, including an attack on a prison in Jawf province that reportedly killed seven people.

The situation escalated further early Tuesday when the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones toward southern Saudi Arabia. The attacks targeted Saudi Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jazan, along with the King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded, including women and children, while fires forced some energy facilities and utilities to suspend operations temporarily.

The renewed fighting effectively ends the relative calm established by the 2022 truce. Since August 23, the escalation inside Yemen has reportedly killed at least 194 people, wounded more than 880 and displaced over 21,000.

Why it matters to the markets

The attacks raise the risk of a broader regional conflict involving Saudi Arabia, the Houthis and, indirectly, Iran. They also create a new threat to global energy supplies.

Saudi Arabia has been routing more oil toward the Red Sea because shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted. Attacks on southern Saudi facilities and Red Sea shipping therefore threaten the alternative route being used to keep crude flowing.

Oil prices have moved to a high today of $94.73. The price is off that high price near $92 currently. The 100 hour moving average comes in at $91.71. That will be a key barometer in the short-term for traders.

The key question now is how aggressively Saudi Arabia responds. A limited response could contain the conflict, but sustained Saudi airstrikes followed by additional Houthi attacks on Aramco facilities or Red Sea shipping would raise the risk of a more serious disruption to global oil supplies.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P 500 analysis shows why bulls don't want to lose this one
item.description:
S&P 500 futures analysis: 7,680 support faces a key test

By Itai Levitan | September 8, 2026 | Analysis snapshot: approximately 12:30 p.m. New York time (UTC-4)

S&P 500 futures are testing support near 7,680 after giving back roughly half of last week’s rebound. On the four-hour chart, the immediate bias is cautious to bearish while price remains below 7,725-7,730. A sustained break below support would increase downside risk, while reclaiming that resistance would improve the recovery case.

Key takeaways for S&P 500 traders
  • Support under pressure: The latest pullback has reached the rising boundary drawn on the chart, near 7,680.
  • Buyers need follow-through: A recovery above 7,725-7,730 would challenge the immediate bearish bias.
  • Confirmation is pending: At the snapshot, futures were near 7,691 and the latest four-hour candle was still forming.

What does the S&P 500 four-hour chart show?

The chart shows a market caught between a rising support line and a falling resistance line. The rising boundary connects the late-July low with the early-September low. The falling boundary tracks the lower major rally peaks since August.

That creates a narrowing triangle-like formation. It tells us where buying and selling pressure are meeting, but the shape alone does not establish which direction will win.

What stands out to me is how much of the latest recovery has already faded. Futures rebounded from approximately 7,619 on September 2 to 7,767 on September 3, a gain of about 148 points. At 7,691, around 76 points, or 51% of that rebound, had been surrendered.

Buyers produced a substantial recovery, but they have struggled to preserve it. That weakens the immediate bullish case without establishing that the entire advance from July has ended.

Why is 7,680 the immediate support test?

The latest candle traded down to 7,680, close to the rising line at the time of the chart capture, before recovering to 7,691. That makes this area the first place to assess whether buyers can interrupt the decline.

A brief move beneath support can reverse quickly. For this four-hour outlook, a completed candle below 7,680, followed by a rebound that fails to recover it, would provide stronger evidence of a breakdown.

The distinction matters: a price touching or briefly crossing a line is an event. Staying below it and failing to regain it shows that the market is beginning to treat the former floor as resistance.

Where could S&P 500 futures head if support fails?

Downside areas to watch below 7,680First support: 7,655-7,Several late-August lows and early-September reactions occurred around this area. It is the first meaningful zone where a decline could slow.Next support: 7,635-7,650This area contains repeated trading and reversals during the September 1-2 selloff and stabilization.Larger downside test: 7,615-7,625This surrounds the early-September low. A sustained break below it would erase the remaining rebound and strengthen the case for a deeper correction.

These are possible reaction areas, not a promise that every level will be reached. If a break below 7,680 quickly reverses and buyers hold back above it, the immediate breakdown case would weaken. A subsequent recovery through 7,725-7,730 would challenge it more decisively.

What would improve the S&P 500 bullish outlook?

The first improvement would be a recovery through 7,705-7,720, where recent trading has repeatedly stalled or reversed. Buyers would then need to reclaim and hold 7,725-7,730, the area around the latest short-term rally highs.

If that happens, attention shifts to 7,745-7,770. This broader resistance zone includes the declining upper boundary near the snapshot and last week’s rebound peak. A bounce into this area could still attract renewed selling.

A sustained move above 7,770, followed by a pullback that holds the breakout, would provide a stronger bullish change. It could bring 7,780-7,800 into view, with the August high area near 7,830-7,840 relevant only if the recovery continues.

A recovery that fails back below 7,725 would lose its first improvement signal. A sustained loss of 7,680 would undermine the support-led rebound scenario.

How can traders use these S&P 500 levels?

I would focus on the reaction after the next test. A failed rebound toward resistance could interest traders assessing a short setup. A dip below 7,680 that is quickly recovered could interest traders watching for a failed breakdown. Either idea still needs an entry, a clear invalidation point and enough potential reward before the next opposing zone.

For example, selling only after price has already reached 7,655-7,670 means initiating a trade at the first mapped support. The bearish outlook may still be relevant, but much of that first opportunity has already passed.

This analysis uses the continuous S&P 500 E-mini futures chart, ES1!. ES contracts provide exposure to S&P 500 performance, as described in CME Group’s product guide. Cash-index, ETF and CFD users should compare the structure with their own product’s prices before applying the levels.

The map should be reassessed if price has already moved well beyond these zones or a newer analysis is available. A four-hour support test can help investors assess near-term market pressure, but does not by itself establish a long-term investment thesis.

For more on confirmation, invalidation and avoiding repeated entries around the same level, read the investingLive tradeCompass guide to using a market map.

Earlier today, I was also tracking crude oil's potential rejection near the $94.60 highs to see if a genuine pullback develops. I am waiting for a definitive break below the $94.14 trigger before considering a conditional short, and I need to see order flow confirm that buyers are actually losing control. This hesitation in the energy market is playing out against a heavy macro backdrop.

As Justin Low at investingLive.com highlighted earlier today, European equities are starting the day on a sluggish, defensive footing as surging oil and climbing yields keep buyers sidelined. Despite these tightening fears, the US outlook remains structurally different.

Eamonn Sheridan noted that UBS expects two more Fed hikes driven by resilient economic growth rather than runaway inflation, keeping their longer-term equity bull case intact. However, consumer sentiment paints a more fragile picture on the ground, with Adam Button from investingLive.com pointing out that the NY Fed survey shows expectations for rising unemployment hitting their highest levels since April 2020.

When we look at the microstructure of the broader markets, the technicals perfectly reflect this fundamental tug-of-war. According to Greg Michalowski's latest index breakdown, the S&P 500 is actively testing critical support at its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, while a sequence of lower highs in the Nasdaq is flashing a clear warning of fading upside momentum.

Greg is tracking a similar structural shift in crypto, noting that Bitcoin's failure to reclaim the $83,916 retracement has shifted the short-term bias lower after aggressive sellers defended the 200-hour moving average.

Finally, for those managing active stock positions, Greg’s follow-up on Bloom Energy's massive 20% technical breakout is a textbook lesson on trailing risk; with the price surging, traders must now define their risk against the 61.8% retracement at $277.58 to protect capital if the setup reverses.

Educational analysis only. Define your maximum loss before entering, and consider partial profits and reduced risk as a trade progresses. Trade at your own risk.

item.title: Bloom Energy Technical view: The price of Bloom Energy is up about 20% since last week's video. What now?
item.description:
In an earlier trading lesson from September 3, I asked a simple question:

Do traders need to know everything about a company before trading its stock?

My answer was no—but that does not mean fundamentals are unimportant.

Understanding what a company does, why its business is attracting attention and what may drive its future growth can help traders develop a directional bias. However, that knowledge alone does not tell you where to enter, where the trade is wrong or how much capital should be placed at risk.

That is where the technicals become essential.

Technical levels provide the trading roadmap. Moving averages, retracement levels, swing areas and previous highs and lows identify where buyers or sellers should show up. More importantly, they give traders levels against which risk can be defined and limited.

You may know everything about a company and still lose money if you buy at the wrong price or fail to control your risk. Conversely, you do not need to know every detail of the business to recognize a favorable technical setup.

The fundamentals tell the company’s story. The technicals tell you how to trade that story—and where to get out if the market proves you wrong.

Bloom Energy provides the lesson

When I published last week’s post and video, Bloom Energy’s stock had been mired in an up-and-down trading range.

That began to change when the price found support against its converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $213.25. Buyers leaned against those moving averages, the price began moving away from them and sellers increasingly turned into buyers.

The upside momentum then carried the price through two important technical levels:

  • The old floor-turned-ceiling near $227.34

  • The 38.2% retracement of the decline from the June 25 all-time high to the July 28 low at $231.66

Those breaks were technically important, but the lesson was not simply that the price was moving higher. The more important point was that the broken levels gave traders a way to define and limit their risk.

For Bloom Energy, the closer risk-defining level was the 38.2% retracement at $231.66. Traders wanting to give the position more room could instead use the old ceiling near $227.34.

The roadmap was straightforward: Stay above those levels and the buyers remain in control. Move back below them and the breakout begins to fail, disappointing the buyers.

What happened next?

The price stayed above both levels, preserving the bullish bias and keeping the buyers in control.

On Friday, the rally continued through the 100-day moving average, currently near $250.37. That break was another important development because moving above the 100-day moving average shifted the longer-term technical bias more in favor of the buyers.

In today’s trading, the price extended above the 50% retracement at $254.62 and then moved through the 61.8% retracement at $277.58. The high reached $283, while the stock is currently trading near $280.44.

As the price moves higher, the risk levels should also be adjusted higher. Traders do not want to allow a winning position to turn into a large losing position.

Close risk can now be defined against:

  • The 61.8% retracement at $277.58

  • The July 9 swing high near $276

  • More conservatively, the rising 100-day moving average near $250.37

The closer levels provide tighter risk but leave less room for normal price volatility. The 100-day moving average gives the position considerably more room, but it also requires accepting greater risk. Each trader must make that decision based on position size, time horizon and risk tolerance.

The technicals told the story

From the converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $213.25, Bloom Energy’s stock has risen by approximately 31%. From the break above the 38.2% retracement at $231.66, the gain has been about 20%.

Did traders need to know every detail about Bloom Energy to participate in that move?

No.

Knowing the company and understanding the fundamental story certainly helps. However, what traders needed most was an understanding of the technical breakout levels—and the discipline to use those same levels to define and limit their risk.

The technicals did not guarantee that the stock would rise. Nothing in trading offers that guarantee. What they did was identify where the buyers were taking control, where momentum was strengthening and where the bullish trade would be proven wrong.

That is the real lesson.

I hope these educational posts help mold your trading mindset toward understanding how price action and technical tools can tell you a great deal about what the market thinks of a company—even if you do not know everything about the company itself.

Know the levels. Define the risk. Follow the price action.

Watch and learn.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD Technicals: The USDCAD is trading lower and dipping below the low from last week
item.description:
The USDCAD moved higher at the end of last week following a stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report and weaker-than-expected Canadian employment data. Fundamentally, that combination should have supported the U.S. dollar against the Canadian dollar.

However, the price action told a different story—and ultimately, price action deals the cards.

The post-jobs rally stalled within a swing area between 1.38669 and 1.3877. Buyers had their shot, but they could not get above that resistance area and stay above it. That failure was the first warning that the fundamental story was not translating into sustained buying.

When a market cannot rally on news that should be bullish, traders need to pay attention. It often signals that the favorable news may already be priced in—or that larger sellers are using the rally as an opportunity to establish positions.

The failed break sent the USDCAD back toward its 200-day moving average at 1.38343. During yesterday’s trading, the price moved above and below that key moving average before finally breaking lower. That tipped the longer-term technical bias more in favor of the sellers.

The downside momentum continued today, taking the pair into a swing area between 1.3765 and 1.3778. The initial test attracted buyers, but the subsequent rebound stalled ahead of the falling 100-hour moving average, currently near 1.38138.

That was another bearish clue.

Not only did the price remain below the broken 200-day moving average, but buyers could not even reach the falling 100-hour moving average before sellers returned. The lower high showed that the sellers were maintaining control of the shorter-term trend.

The price subsequently rotated back toward the 1.3765–1.3778 swing area during the North American session. This time, the floor gave way, with the USDCAD reaching 1.3760—its lowest level since August 21.

The price has bounced modestly, but it is so far trying to remain below—or within—the broken swing area. That area is now the key short-term barometer. Remember, old support often becomes new resistance after it is broken.

For traders, the technical roadmap is relatively straightforward:

  • Staying below the 1.3765–1.3778 swing area keeps the sellers in control and the downside as the favored path of least resistance.

  • The next important target comes near 1.3732. That level represents both the August swing low and a rising trend line, increasing its technical importance.

  • A break below 1.3732 would open the door toward the next swing area near 1.3710.

  • If buyers are going to take back some control, they must first reclaim 1.3778. Above that, the 61.8% retracement near 1.3793 would become the next hurdle, followed by the falling 100-hour moving average near 1.38138.

The stronger U.S. jobs data and weaker Canadian employment report may have given USDCAD buyers what looked like the strongest fundamental hand. However, they failed to play it successfully.

For now, the technical hand belongs to the sellers—and they are holding the strongest cards.

item.title: The S&P and Nasdaq Technicals: What are the charts telling traders in the broader US stock indices NOW?
item.description:
Both the broader S&P and Nasdaq indices are trading lower on the day, with declines of around 0.45%. The weakness has both indices moving closer to key hourly moving averages that could help determine whether buyers remain in control—or whether the short-term bias begins to shift more firmly to the downside.

S&P tests its 100- and 200-hour moving averages

For the S&P index, the price is testing both its 100- and 200-hour moving averages in early North American trading:

  • 100-hour moving average: 7,689.86

  • 200-hour moving average: 7,676

Those moving averages represent an important technical barometer for buyers and sellers. Holding above them would give buyers some hope that the current decline is simply a corrective move within the broader upward trend. The low price for the day just reached 7675.69 right near the 200 hour moving average level.

Conversely, a sustained move below both moving averages would tilt the short-term bias back to the downside. It would also tell traders that buyers are losing control of a support area that has helped define the trend.

That distinction is important. Moving averages do not predict where the market must go, but they provide traders with levels where risk can be defined. Buyers looking to lean against the area want to see the price remain above it. If the price breaks below and stays below, those buyers may be forced to exit, while sellers become more confident.

Lower highs signal fading upside momentum

Looking at the broader price action, the S&P broke higher in early August and eventually reached an all-time high of 7,815.54. Since then, however, the subsequent highs have been lower:

  • All-time high: 7,815.54

  • Late-August high: 7,771.48

  • September high: 7,756.00

The sequence of lower highs is a modest negative. It shows that buyers have continued to push the index higher, but each rally has stalled sooner than the one before it.

That does not guarantee a larger decline, but when lower highs are combined with a break below important moving-average support, the technical picture becomes more bearish.

If the S&P moves below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages—and can stay below—the next downside target would be the swing area between 7,577.92 and 7,617.37.

That area would become the next key test. Buyers would likely try to establish support there, while sellers would look for a break below it to open the door to additional downside momentum.

Nasdaq remains above its hourly moving averages—for now

The Nasdaq index is also moving closer to its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, although it remains above both levels:

  • 100-hour moving average: 26,279.68

  • 200-hour moving average: 26,216.81

  • Today’s low: 26,341.17

Because the Nasdaq remains above both moving averages, buyers retain more control in the short term. However, the cushion is narrowing.

Staying above the 100-hour moving average would keep the immediate bias more positive. A break below that level would increase the focus on the 200-hour moving average. If both moving averages are broken, the technical bias would shift more decisively in favor of sellers.

Nasdaq’s lower highs are also a warning

Like the S&P, the Nasdaq has also been making lower highs:

  • All-time high from early June: 27,190.21

  • August high: 26,875.52

  • September high: 26,644.00

The Nasdaq is therefore still well below its record high, unlike the S&P, which set its all-time high more recently.

The declining highs from June into August and September indicate that buyers have been unable to regain the momentum needed to challenge the record. That makes the approaching hourly moving averages even more important. If those levels hold, buyers would have another opportunity to rebuild upside momentum. If they break, the lower-high pattern would receive additional confirmation.

What traders should watch now

For both indices, the technical story is centered on the same question: Can the hourly moving averages hold?

The S&P is already testing its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, making it the more immediate focus. The Nasdaq remains above its corresponding levels, but it is moving closer.

The educational lesson is that traders should watch how the market behaves around a key level—not simply whether the level is touched. A brief move below a moving average followed by a quick recovery can signal a failed break. By contrast,ly, a move below followed by failed attempts to recover above the moving averages would give sellers greater confidence.

For now, the S&P is at a key decision point. The Nasdaq is approaching one. The price action around these hourly moving averages should help determine whether today’s weakness remains a modest correction or develops into a more meaningful downside move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin technicals: The price of bitcoin is lower on the day and the technical tilt is modestly lower
item.description:
Bitcoin’s technical picture is starting to shift back to the downside after buyers failed to extend the recent rally through an important area of resistance on the daily chart.

Daily chart: The recovery runs into resistance

Starting with the broader daily chart, as a review Bitcoin’s rebound higher accelerated after the price moved back above its 100-day and 200-day moving averages back on August 19. That breakout gave buyers the technical go-ahead to push higher.

However, the rally stalled within a key swing area between $80,560 and $82,833 toward the end of August and into September too. That zone has repeatedly attracted sellers since that time. The swing area was defined by swing lows and highs going back to November 2025.  

Just above that swing area is another important target: the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the October 2025 high, which comes in at $83,916.

Why is that retracement important?

When a market suffers a significant decline, the 38.2% retracement is often the first major test of whether a rebound is developing into something more substantial. If buyers cannot push through that level, the recovery can remain nothing more than a correction within the broader decline.

In this case, Bitcoin could not get through either the $80,560–$82,833 swing area or the 38.2% retracement at $83,916. That failure is a modest technical negative and has helped shift the focus back toward the downside.

For buyers to regain greater control on the daily chart, they would need to move above $82,833 and then extend through $83,916. Until that happens, the sellers remain in play.

Hourly chart: The short-term bias turns lower

Drilling down to the hourly chart, today’s price action has taken Bitcoin below its 200-hour moving average at $79,007.

The break by itself was bearish, but what happened afterward provided additional confirmation.

Bitcoin staged a corrective move higher a few hours ago and retested the 200-hour moving average from below. Instead of moving back above it, the price found willing sellers and subsequently extended to new session lows.

That is a classic example of former support becoming resistance.

The 100-hour moving average at $79,538 is also positioned just above the 200-hour moving average. Together, those two moving averages now form an important resistance cluster between approximately $79,007 and $79,538. Staying below gives the sellers the advantage and opens the door toward the recent lows in the consolidation area at $76,229 and below that at $75,568 (lows from September 2 and August 23 respectively).

What would change the bearish bias?

As long as Bitcoin remains below both hourly moving averages, sellers have more control over the short-term direction.

The technical roadmap is straightforward:

  • Staying below $79,007–$79,538 keeps the short-term bias tilted to the downside.

  • Moving back above both moving averages would weaken the bearish bias and give buyers another opportunity.

  • A sustained move above $80,560 would improve the picture further.

  • Breaking above $82,833, followed by the 38.2% retracement at $83,916, would be required to give buyers firmer control on the daily chart.

The lesson for traders is that moving averages are not merely lines on a chart. What matters is how the price behaves around them. Bitcoin broke below the 200-hour moving average, retested it, and found sellers. That price action gives traders a clearly defined bearish bias and, equally important, a clearly defined level where that bias would begin to change.

item.description:
The US entered Labor Day with average gasoline prices at $4.14 a gallon, almost $1 higher than a year ago, while diesel hit a record $5.85 as the Middle East crisis drags on.

Despite the US president claiming full control over the Strait of Hormuz in early August, only about 10 commercial vessels a day have passed through the strait over the past 10 days, the lowest level since May and down from more than 15 just days earlier as attacks in the area picked up.

Moreover, Yemen’s Houthis attacked energy facilities and cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, prompting the Saudi Energy Ministry to say that operations at some energy facilities had been suspended.

And then there’s the Russia-Ukraine war, with Ukraine continuing to target Russian refineries.

Why haven’t oil prices jumped above $100 a barrel?

On the one hand, alternative routes are helping keep supplies moving through Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, and Egypt, along with rising output from the US, Canada, and Guyana. On the other hand, weaker Chinese imports and softer global demand are helping keep prices in check.

Still, Goldman Sachs warns that oil could jump to $120 if attacks on tankers intensify and export disruptions worsen, subsequently pushing up the cost of everything from oil-based products to transportation and, eventually, food and delivery. 

Hence, the risk of tighter monetary policy from central banks, including the Fed, which has around a 60% chance of hiking rates next week following stronger-than-expected labor data. If Friday’s August inflation also comes in hotter than expected, those odds would rise even further. 

In Europe, with inflation rising to 3.3% in August from 2.9% in July, markets are pricing in another ECB rate hike from 2.25% to 2.50% at Thursday’s meeting. As for President Christine Lagarde, she will most likely avoid giving any direct hints on further moves, stressing that they will depend on the incoming data. 

In Japan, the BOJ is also expected to raise its key rate to 1.25% at its September 17–18 meeting, keeping its hawkish stance and adding to the yen’s recent strength, which is putting pressure on the USD JPY pair.

Overall, the mood has shifted back toward higher rates, which is why we’re seeing more nervousness in global bond markets. The longer yields stay high, the greater the risk of money moving out of riskier assets and into bonds. For now, though, markets are holding up well.

item.title: A-Book vs B-Book: How Brokers Actually Manage Your Trades
item.description:
Quick answer

The usual explanation is simple. An A-book broker hedges a client trade with a liquidity provider, while a B-book broker keeps the exposure and may benefit if the client loses.

That explanation is useful as a starting point, but it is not how most established CFD brokers manage risk in practice. A CFD broker remains the client's contractual counterparty. Separately, the broker may offset opposing client positions, hedge some or all of its net exposure externally, or retain a limited amount of risk within defined controls.

In practice, many established CFD brokers use some form of hybrid or portfolio-level risk management. They manage the combined exposure created by thousands of trades rather than mechanically sending every individual order to a liquidity provider or simply betting against every client.

Base Markets is a useful example. It manages exposure primarily at aggregate portfolio level, considering exposure across its client book, internally offsetting opposing positions, and managing the residual through external hedging and controlled risk retention. Base's decision to offset, hedge, or retain the resulting exposure does not, in itself, change the pricing and execution terms applicable to the client's account.

That distinction matters. The more useful questions are not whether a broker uses a fashionable label, but whether its pricing is clear, its execution is fair, its risk is controlled, and it can meet withdrawals when clients are profitable.

What this guide covers

This guide explains:

  • what the industry usually means by A-book and B-book
  • what legally and operationally happens when a CFD trade is opened
  • how internalisation, netting, and external hedging work together
  • where genuine conflicts of interest can arise
  • what traders should ask a broker before depositing
  • how Base Markets applies these principles in practice

A-book and B-book: the conventional explanation

In retail trading, A-book and B-book are informal industry terms. They are not precise legal classifications, and different brokers sometimes use them differently.

What is usually meant by A-book?

An A-book model is commonly described as straight-through processing, or STP. The broker receives a client order and creates an equivalent hedge with a bank, prime broker, non-bank market maker, or another liquidity provider.

If a client buys 10 lots of EUR/USD, the broker buys 10 lots externally. The client's profit or loss is substantially offset by the external hedge, leaving the broker to earn from commission, spread markup, financing, or other disclosed charges.

This is often marketed as if the client's trade itself has been passed into the market. With an over-the-counter CFD, that description is incomplete. The client's contract remains with the broker. The external transaction is the broker's own hedge of the exposure created by that contract.

What is usually meant by B-book?

A B-book model is commonly described as the broker retaining the risk. If the client buys 10 lots, the broker does not necessarily create an equivalent external hedge. The broker remains economically exposed to the client's result.

If the client loses, retained client trading losses may benefit the broker. If the client wins, the broker must pay the profit from its own resources. This creates a potential conflict, but it does not by itself prove that the client received an unfair price or execution.

The simple comparison

What actually happens when you trade a CFD?

When a client buys a CFD, the broker is the contractual counterparty to that CFD. The client is not normally acquiring the underlying currency, index, commodity, or share from the external market. The broker calculates the client's profit or loss by reference to the relevant market price and settles the CFD under its terms.

The trade creates market exposure for the broker. The broker then decides how to manage that exposure. It may:

  • offset it against a client position in the opposite direction
  • hedge it with one or more external liquidity providers
  • retain it temporarily or permanently within an approved risk limit
  • use a combination of all three

These are risk-management decisions made behind the client contract. They should not determine whether the client receives fair pricing, appropriate execution, or access to valid profits.

This is why statements such as "your order is sent directly to the market" should be read carefully. They may describe the broker's hedging process, but they do not alter the legal structure of an OTC CFD. ECN, STP, agency, A-book, and B-book can be useful shorthand, but none of them replaces a clear explanation of who the counterparty is and how the broker manages exposure.

One client, two clients, and thousands of clients

The mechanics become clearer when viewed at portfolio level.

One client buys 100 lots

Assume one client buys 100 lots of EUR/USD and there are no other relevant positions. A broker that does not want the directional risk can buy 100 lots from a liquidity provider.

Suppose, purely for illustration, the client pays USD 7 per lot round turn and the external hedge costs the broker USD 5 per lot. The broker's gross difference is USD 2 per lot before technology, staffing, regulation, payments, bad debt, financing, and other operating costs.

The important commercial point is that a durable broker does not need the client to lose. It can earn a fair amount from repeated trading activity. A profitable client who continues trading for years can be more valuable than a client who loses a USD 500 balance once and leaves.

For Base, the better commercial outcome is to earn a fair amount from a client who trades for years, rather than make a larger one-off gain when that client loses everything and leaves.

Base applies that principle through transparent pricing. On FX, Base Zero charges USD 2 per side, or USD 4 round turn per standard lot. The commercial objective is recurring, clearly disclosed trading revenue and a long-term relationship, not dependence on an individual client's loss.

One client buys 100 lots and another sells 100 lots

Now assume one client is long 100 lots and another is short 100 lots in the same instrument. Their positions create no net directional exposure for the broker at that moment.

If the market rises, the broker owes the long client and receives the corresponding loss from the short client. If the market falls, the economic result reverses. The broker effectively administers the two contracts and charges each client the disclosed trading costs.

Hedging both positions separately would create external commission, spread, financing, and margin costs without reducing the broker's net market risk. Internally offsetting them is therefore not automatically a trick or a bet against either trader. It is a rational way to manage a portfolio.

This process is usually called internalisation or netting. It can improve the broker's economics and reduce unnecessary dependence on external liquidity. It can also provide additional capacity because the broker does not need to send two offsetting positions into the market simply to cancel them out.

Thousands of clients trade continuously

Real broker books are far more dynamic. Thousands of clients open, close, increase, reduce, and reverse positions across many instruments and time horizons. Some exposures offset immediately. Others remain unmatched for seconds, hours, or longer.

Imagine clients are collectively long 1,000 lots and short 1,000.01 lots. The broker's net exposure is only 0.01 lots. It may decide that this difference is too small to hedge efficiently, is within its risk tolerance, or is likely to be offset by the next incoming order.

Now imagine the book is long 1,000 lots and short 900 lots. The broker has a net long exposure of 100 lots. It can hedge all of that residual, hedge part of it, or retain it within approved limits. The decision may depend on volatility, liquidity, concentration, event risk, available LP credit, and the broker's capital.

This portfolio approach explains why a broker's headline hedging percentage can be misleading. In the 1,000-lot long and 900-lot short example, hedging 100 lots represents only 5.3% of the 1,900 lots of gross positions, but it represents 100% of the broker's net directional exposure. The denominator matters.

It also explains why asking whether a particular trade was A-booked or B-booked may produce a false sense of certainty. An individual client position can be internally offset today, part of an external portfolio hedge a moment later, and offset again as the book changes.

How CFD brokers make money

A broker can earn revenue from several sources, including:

  • commission charged per lot or as a percentage of value
  • a disclosed markup within the spread
  • overnight financing charges
  • urrency conversion and other clearly stated fees
  • the net result of market exposure retained by the broker

The first four sources can support a straightforward, repeatable business. A broker provides access, technology, execution, risk infrastructure, payments, and service in exchange for transparent charges.

Retained exposure is different because its result varies with client performance and the market. It can produce gains or losses for the broker. A properly managed firm treats that as a controlled portfolio risk, not as permission to interfere with a client trade.

Why internalisation is not automatically bad

Internalisation is sometimes presented as evidence that the broker is trading against its clients. That is too simplistic.

The broker is already the contractual counterparty to the CFD. Whether it hedges the resulting exposure is a separate treasury and risk decision. If opposing client positions naturally offset, avoiding two unnecessary external hedges can reduce transaction costs, LP margin requirements, and operational friction.

It can also make more liquidity available to clients than the broker could obtain from a single external venue at a particular moment. The broker can combine internal flow with multiple liquidity providers and use its own risk capacity to support execution.

The client should care about the outcome: Was the price derived fairly? Was the order handled consistently? Was any slippage genuine and applied according to disclosed rules? Can the broker meet the resulting obligation if the client wins?

Internalisation becomes a problem when the broker's economic interest in a client loss begins to influence those answers.

Where the conflict becomes unacceptable

A retained-risk model creates a potential conflict because the broker may benefit economically when clients lose. Potential conflicts exist in many financial businesses. The test is how they are controlled.

The line is crossed when a broker uses its control over the trading environment to manufacture or increase client losses. Warning signs can include:

  • unjustified or consistently asymmetric slippage
  • prices that depart materially from credible market references without explanation
  • arbitrary spread widening unrelated to market conditions
  • selective delays or rejection of profitable orders
  • cancellation of legitimate profitable trades after the event
  • withdrawal obstruction or pressure to keep funds in the account
  • different execution treatment based on whether the client is winning

These are not theoretical concerns. Regulators have pursued CFD businesses for systemic unconscionable conduct involving manipulation of client trades and obstruction of withdrawals. One documented example is the Australian Securities and Investments Commission's 2024 Federal Court case.

The lesson is not that every broker retaining exposure behaves improperly. It is that execution controls, financial strength, governance, and withdrawal conduct matter more than a marketing label.

Why the broker's capital matters

External hedging requires capital. A broker may offer a client 500:1 leverage while receiving only 100:1 from its liquidity provider.

For a simplified USD 100,000 position, the client may post USD 200 of margin at 500:1. To create the same external hedge at 100:1, the broker may need to post USD 1,000 with its LP. That is five times the client's margin. The USD 1,000 is collateral committed while the hedge remains open, rather than a trading cost, and is normally released when the hedge is closed. At 100 lots, the simplified requirement becomes USD 20,000 from clients against USD 100,000 at the LP.

Actual requirements vary by asset, counterparty, concentration, volatility, and credit arrangement, but the principle is important. A broker can promise high leverage more easily than it can fund a large hedging programme.

Retaining exposure also requires financial strength. If clients are profitable in aggregate, the broker must pay them. Sharp events such as the removal of the Swiss franc floor in 2015 can create concentrated gains and losses quickly. A weak broker may respond by delaying withdrawals, disputing legitimate trades, asking clients not to withdraw, or failing altogether.

Base Markets is majority-owned by an investment fund. That financial backing matters because external hedging requires properly funded LP accounts, while retained exposure requires the broker to have sufficient liquidity to meet profitable client positions and withdrawals.

Financial backing is not a substitute for risk controls, and regulation is the starting point rather than the entire story. It does, however, help distinguish a broker built to operate through difficult markets from one dependent on the next wave of client deposits.

Can you identify an A-book or B-book broker from the platform?

Not reliably.

Variable spreads, commission-based accounts, positive or negative slippage, re-quotes, fast execution, and MT5 Depth of Market do not prove whether the broker hedged the resulting exposure externally. Those features may say something about pricing or execution, but they do not reveal the broker's complete risk book.

A "raw" account does not prove agency execution. A fixed spread does not prove B-booking. A liquidity-provider logo does not show which exposures are hedged, when they are hedged, or in what amount. Even a broker that hedges extensively may aggregate transactions rather than replicate each client order one for one.

The better approach is simpler: ask the broker.

Traders should not need to conduct forensic analysis on an MT5 account to understand a broker's business model. They should be able to ask the broker and receive a straight answer.

Useful questions include:

  1. Are you the contractual counterparty to my CFD?
  2. Do you manage exposure at individual trade or aggregate portfolio level?
  3. Do opposing client positions offset internally?
  4. How do you manage residual exposure and concentration risk?
  5. Does execution or pricing change according to how my exposure is managed?
  6. What are the total trading costs, including commission, spread, financing, and conversion?
  7. How are client funds held, and what is the normal withdrawal process?
  8. Who owns and finances the brokerage?

A credible broker may not publish its liquidity counterparties, hedge thresholds, or real-time exposure. Those can be commercially sensitive risk-management details. It should still be able to explain its model clearly, identify its regulator and legal entity, publish its charges, and describe how it handles execution and withdrawals.

Separately agreed institutional hedging arrangements may be considered where legally, operationally, and commercially appropriate, subject to liquidity, margin, volume, and reporting requirements.

How Base Markets applies the model

Base Markets is regulated by the Financial Services Commission of Mauritius under licence number GB25204723.

Base's approach can be summarised plainly:

  • Base is the contractual counterparty to client CFDs.
  • Opposing client positions may be internally offset at aggregate level.
  • Residual exposure is externally hedged or retained within defined risk limits.
  • Base's decision to offset, hedge, or retain the resulting exposure does not, in itself, change the pricing and execution terms applicable to the client's account.
  • Base manages exposure primarily at aggregate portfolio level and does not alter a client's applicable pricing or execution solely because the client is profitable or because the resulting exposure is hedged or retained.
  • The preferred commercial model is transparent trading revenue from clients who continue to trade.

This is consistent with the broader Base proposition. The firm competes on clear total pricing, credible liquidity, execution oversight, straightforward funding and withdrawals, and access to people who understand the trading environment.

It does not claim that trading is easy or that clients will necessarily be profitable. CFDs are high-risk products and most retail traders lose money. The point is narrower and more important: a broker does not need to design its business around making an individual client fail.

Four common myths

Myth 1: A-book means there is no conflict

An external hedge can reduce market risk, but the broker still controls pricing, execution rules, margin, and the client relationship. A label does not guarantee good conduct.

Myth 2: B-book means the broker is manipulating trades

Retaining exposure creates a potential conflict, not proof of abuse. Fair pricing, consistent execution, adequate capital, and reliable withdrawals remain the proper tests.

Myth 3: Raw spreads or MT5 Depth of Market prove A-book execution

They do not. They show elements of the client trading environment, not the broker's complete aggregate exposure or external hedge activity.

Myth 4: A low hedge percentage means most client trades are being bet against

Not necessarily. Gross client positions may offset substantially. A small hedge as a percentage of gross volume can cover all of the remaining net directional risk.

Frequently asked questions

Is A-book always safer than B-book?

No. The label alone does not establish financial strength, execution quality, governance, or withdrawal reliability. A poorly capitalised A-book broker can still fail, while a well-capitalised hybrid broker can manage risk responsibly.

Does a broker profit when I lose?

It may benefit from losses on exposure it retains, but it may also lose when retained clients win. Many brokers earn primarily from spreads, commission, financing, and other fees while managing aggregate market exposure separately.

Does internalisation affect my price?

It should not result in unfair treatment. Base's decision to offset, hedge, or retain the resulting exposure does not, in itself, change the pricing and execution terms applicable to the client's account.

Can I see whether my exact trade was hedged?

Usually not from a retail platform. Hedging may occur at aggregate portfolio level and may change as other clients trade. Ask the broker how its overall process works.

Why would a broker retain any exposure?

Tiny residual positions may be uneconomic to hedge, offsetting flow may arrive quickly, and limited exposure may fall within an approved risk appetite. The issue is whether the risk is controlled and adequately funded.

What should make me cautious?

Unclear total costs, unexplained execution differences, withdrawal pressure, evasive answers about the legal entity or regulator, and extravagant promises unsupported by the actual trading product should all prompt further investigation.

Conclusion: judge the broker, not the label

A-book and B-book are convenient shorthand, but they often obscure more than they reveal. A CFD broker remains the client's counterparty. Behind that contract, the broker can offset client flow, hedge externally, retain controlled exposure, or combine all three.

The real dividing line is not between a pure A-book and a pure B-book. It is between brokers that manage exposure professionally and treat clients fairly, and brokers that use opaque pricing, weak capital, or withdrawal obstruction to protect themselves.

Base Markets offers a direct version of the hybrid model: aggregate the book, offset opposing flow, manage the residual, keep risk-management decisions separate from the pricing and execution terms applicable to each client's account, and earn transparent revenue from long-term trading activity.

For traders, the practical test is equally direct. Understand what you pay. Assess the execution you receive. Ask how the broker manages risk. Check who regulates, owns, and finances it. Then judge whether it behaves like a business built to be there when markets, and clients, are profitable.

Risk warning: Trading CFDs carries a high level of risk to capital and may not be suitable for all investors. Trade only with money you can afford to lose, ensure you understand the risks, and seek independent advice where necessary.

item.title: Bitcoin has already won its battle, whereas Ethereum is only starting its own
item.description:
When it comes to cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin and Ethereum are two of the major household names.

The former has spent more than a decade in answering one fundamental question: Can cryptocurrencies really become an institutional asset class?

And the answer to that seems to be increasingly a yes.

But for Ethereum, the challenge is very much a different one.

The cryptocurrency has enjoyed a good summer, outpacing Bitcoin in terms of gains. In fact, the ETH/BTC ratio has climbed back above 0.031 - the first time in four months. Adding to that, money is beginning to also follow the price.

US spot Ether ETFs attracted around $1.85 billion in August, their strongest month in about a year. That adds to yet another flashpoint where investors are not quite treating it merely as a leveraged bet on Bitcoin.

And this is where things might get a little more interesting for Ethereum in the big picture.

Bitcoin has already found its place, Ethereum not quite

The institutional pitch for Bitcoin is relatively simple and straighforward. Scarce supply. Decentralised monetary asset. Digital gold.

Whether or not investors agree with the valuation is another question, but Wall Street definitely understands what it is supposed to be.

In the case of Ethereum, that is one that has always been harder to package.

It is simultaneously a blockchain, settlement layer, collateral asset, and infrastructure underpinning stablecoins, tokenised securities and decentralised finance. That all sounds very messy and one can argue that the complexity is what has been a valuation handicap for Ethereum.

But as time goes on, could that underlying complexity be the very thing that changes the narrative for Ethereum?

Imagine this. Ethereum hosts roughly $156 billion of stablecoin assets, all the while institutional adoption through ETFs continues to deepen. And if tokenisation and on-chain finance continue expanding, investors may increasingly value Ethereum as exposure to the infrastructure underneath that ecosystem.

Changing the equation takes time

If Ethereum keeps rising merely because Bitcoin rises, nothing fundamental has changed.

But perhaps another way to look at it is not through the lens of ETH/USD but perhaps ETH/BTC.

So if ETH/BTC begins trending sustainably higher while ETF demand continues building, that would suggest genuine capital rotation and a considerable reassessment of Ethereum's relative value.

It might be premature but the price movements this past summer may have provided a little glimpse of that. In looking at the cryptocurrency space, Ethereum does not need to replace Bitcoin. It simply needs to prove that it no longer needs Bitcoin to justify its own investment case.

If Ethereum can continue outperforming while institutional flows persist through a challenging macro backdrop, the market may be witnessing something more important than another altcoin rally.

It is early days and the cryptocurrency market is also still transitioning to a more mature phase. Things move faster here than in traditional markets but with all things, sometimes it still takes time.

Whether Ethereum can truly rise up to live up to the billing will also highly depend on the ever changing landscape in cryptocurrencies but also the world of finance.

But for now, at least one thing is clear. Bitcoin's institutionalisation was about proving that cryptocurrencies could become an asset. Ethereum's case is more about proving that a blockchain can become financial infrastructure - and be valued accordingly.

And that battle seems to have only just begun.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: How oil prices influence inflation, inflation expectations and monetary policy
item.description:
Oil prices are among the most important variables for inflation. A sustained rise in crude prices can push headline inflation higher directly, but its impact can extend beyond energy prices by influencing inflation expectations. One useful market-based measure of those expectations is the breakeven inflation rate.

What are breakeven inflation rates?

A breakeven inflation rate is the difference between the yield on a conventional Treasury bond and the yield on an inflation-protected Treasury of the same maturity.

For example, taking the 10-year breakeven, which is generally used as benchmark: 

10-year breakeven = 10-year Treasury yield − 10-year TIPS yield

The result represents the average annual inflation rate that would make an investor indifferent between holding the two securities until maturity, although it is important to remember that breakevens also contain inflation-risk and liquidity premia and are therefore not a pure measure of expected inflation. 

Nonetheless, breakevens are particularly useful for monitoring how financial markets are pricing the inflation outlook. Historically, there has been a meaningful positive relationship between oil prices and inflation breakevens. 

Chart: WTI crude oil (blue) vs 10-year breakeven (red)

Why do oil prices matter for inflation?

The most obvious channel is direct energy inflation. When crude oil rises, other energy products generally become more expensive. Since energy is part of consumer price indexes, higher oil prices can lift headline CPI directly.

Oil is also an important input into transportation, manufacturing, chemicals and other parts of the economy. Higher energy costs can therefore increase businesses' costs, which may eventually be passed on to consumers through higher prices and impact core CPI.

There is also an expectations channel. If consumers and businesses believe that higher oil prices will persist, they may begin to expect higher overall inflation. Workers may demand higher wages, while companies may become more willing to raise prices. These second-round effects can make an initially energy-driven inflation shock more persistent.

Chart: WTI crude oil (blue) vs US headline CPI (red)

Monetary policy impact

The relationship between oil prices and inflation is especially important for central banks, as they have a mandate to keep inflation stable over the medium term, generally around a target of 2% per year. Central banks usually ignore supply-driven shocks because most of the time they are temporary. They push up headline inflation, but don't have much impact on core inflation. What central banks care more about is whether inflation expectations remain anchored.

A sustained increase in oil prices that pushes up inflation expectations is much more significant for a central bank because it raises the risk of second-round inflation effects. That can complicate the central bank's job of keeping inflation stable and require a monetary policy action. Policymakers must consider whether an energy shock is temporary or whether it risks becoming embedded in broader inflation.

When a central bank adopts a hawkish bias to combat energy-driven inflation, inflation expectations are generally kept in check and don't rise too much as markets expect rate hikes to eventually lower inflation. Conversely, if a central bank keeps a neutral or even dovish bias despite persistently higher energy prices, inflation expectations generally rise faster and the risk of second-round effects rises substantially. 

Conclusion

Central banks cannot directly control oil prices, but they can influence how an oil shock affects the broader economy. Higher energy prices initially push inflation higher from the supply side, but monetary policy can respond by weakening demand through tighter financial conditions, helping prevent the shock from becoming embedded in underlying inflation and inflation expectations.

This creates an important interaction between oil and monetary policy. Oil prices can push inflation higher, while the central bank can counteract the resulting inflationary pressure by cooling demand. The more persistent the oil shock and the stronger its impact on inflation expectations, the greater the pressure on the central bank to keep policy restrictive.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: The bond market continues to tighten the screws, and everything else is feeling it
item.description:
It's a new week but once again we are starting to see bond yields push higher again. And if this keeps up, it will be increasingly more difficult for broader markets to ignore.

10-year Treasury yields are touching 4.80% again, its highest levels since 2023, while 30-year yields in the US are starting to nudge back closer to 5.30%. It's a similar story elsewhere around the globe as borrowing costs in the likes of the UK, Japan, and Germany are all hovering around multi-year or multi-decade highs. Today itself, 10-year Germany bond yields are back at 3.39% - the highest since 2011.

This is all coming together amid a combination of fiscal and inflation risks, which is threatening to alter the landscape of the market. Here is more context from last week: The tectonic shift that is taking place in the bond market

And this week we're also seeing oil prices sure higher again, adding more upside risks to the inflation outlook. And it comes in a tricky time for markets, just before the US CPI report on Friday as well as key central bank decisions with the ECB, Fed, and BOJ all set to be tested.

The stock market is starting to feel the pinch

S&P 500 futures are down by 0.4% with Dow futures down 0.9% on the day now. Tech shares are also slipping with Nasdaq futures down 0.2% currently.

It's shaping up to be a poor start to the new week upon the return from the long weekend.

Higher Treasury yields raise the discount rate used to value future earnings, and that is particularly problematic for richly valued growth and tech stocks. The closer that 10-year yields move towards the psychologically important 5% level, the harder it becomes to justify elevated equity multiples when investors can earn attractive returns from government bonds with considerably less risk.

That being said, this does not automatically mean that stocks will collapse right there and then. Ultimately, the combination investors do not want is higher yields without stronger growth.

In time, we will see how that balance plays out.

Gold faces up against an uncomfortable environment

The precious metal has been caught in a bit of a tug-of-war this month, needing to weigh up the changing dynamics in broader markets.

Higher real yields are traditionally a headwind for gold because they increase the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. However, gold has been able to stay resilient because of the very same factors driving the push up in yields.

Inflation worries, geopolitical tensions, and sovereign debt sustainability concerns are all key factors that feed into demand for hard assets like gold - especially the latter.

With fiscal risks mounting across many major economies and central bank demand still being sustained for the most part, gold remains an attractive proposition in a world which is experiencing quite the shift from a debt and macroeconomic standpoint.

The bigger message from the bond market

In the big picture, the level in which the Fed sets its policy rate may not be as important as where investors are willing to fund governments for ten or thirty years.

Central banks just simply cannot fully control the term premium demanded by investors in holding bonds. And this is something that the bond vigilantes have often taken advantage of.

If long-term yields keep climbing toward 5% and beyond, the bond market effectively starts tightening financial conditions on its own.

And that is when higher yields are no longer just another market move. They are arguably becoming the macro variable that everything else has to trade around.

It's definitely some food for thought as things continue down this road as we begin to turn the corner to the final quarter of the year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil prices extend gains as Yemen's Houthis threaten broader Saudi operation after attacks hit energy sites
item.description:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched a series of attacks against targets in southern Saudi Arabia, including energy facilities, military sites and other strategic locations, in a fresh escalation in regional tensions.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said several energy facilities and installations in the kingdom’s southern region were targeted, causing fires and temporarily halting some operations. Emergency teams were deployed to contain the fires and secure the affected sites.

Saudi authorities said the attacks targeted areas including Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, with the Saudi-led coalition reporting that 73 people were injured.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they used drones and ballistic missiles against Saudi targets. The group said it had targeted Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as a military airbase in Khamis Mushait.

The Houthis would also announce a broader military operation deep inside Saudi territory, raising the risk of further attacks against the kingdom's energy infrastructure.

The escalation comes after renewed fighting in Yemen and follows reports of Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launching offensives against Houthi positions. The Houthis have said their latest attacks are retaliation for Saudi military actions in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks as a dangerous escalation and said it would take the necessary measures to defend its sovereignty. The Saudi-led coalition also vowed to respond firmly.

The developments are particularly significant for oil markets given Saudi Arabia's role as the world's largest oil exporter. The attacks come amid already elevated geopolitical risks in the Middle East, with oil prices approaching $100 a barrel as concerns over supply disruptions intensify.

WTI crude oil broke above the July high and it's now trading at the highest level since June. The next target should be the swing high around the 97.00 handle, with a break above that level taking us to $100.

item.title: USD/JPY selloff extends further as Yen hits seven-month high; US CPI and BoJ in focus next
item.description:
FUNDAMENTAL OVERVIEW

 

USD:

The US dollar spiked to the upside on Friday after the US NFP report showed job growth in August almost tripling the consensus estimate of 56K. The dollar gains didn’t last long, though, as most of the NFP-driven moves got faded thereafter.

This happened because the market focus was not on the NFP report, but on the CPI. The market pays attention to the data that the central bank is focused on, and the Federal Reserve is currently focused on inflation.

In fact, just a day before the NFP report, Fed’s Waller mentioned that he would support keeping interest rates unchanged at the upcoming FOMC meeting, but a hot CPI would make him consider a rate hike.

This week, all eyes will be on the US CPI data. Unless, we get some surprising breakthrough in US-Iran relations, the price action will likely remain mostly rangebound or a bit positive for the greenback as traders at some point might start hedging into the CPI release.

A soft or in-line CPI will likely weaken the dollar as Fed’s Waller mentioned that he won’t consider a rate hike unless we get a hot CPI. Conversely, an upside surprise in core monthly inflation data will likely trigger another rally on a hawkish repricing.

JPY:

On the JPY side, the currency reportedly strengthened on the back of a hawkish repricing following BoJ Takata’s comments. I remain sceptical that was the culprit, though, given that Takata has been the most hawkish member for a long time and there’s been minimal repricing in interest rate expectations by looking at overnight index swaps.

More likely, we’ve seen deleveraging in carry trades ahead of the BoJ rate decision given that short positioning on the yen has been pretty extreme.

BoJ Governor Ueda has also commented on monetary policyrecently but didn’t offer anything new. In my opinion, his comments were actually a bit less hawkish as he mentioned that the BoJ will assess the cumulative impact of its previous rate hikes on the economy and stressed that they have already raised rates five times during the current tightening cycle.

Now, the September rate hike is already priced in, so that won’t move the market much. Traders will be focused on forward guidance and signals about the future tightening pace. The uptrend in USD/JPY is unlikely to change without a dovish repricing in Fed interest rate expectations or a faster BoJ tightening pace.
